title: Is Sam Mendes one of the great directors or just good?

commenti.body: [removed]
[removed]

I'd say he's a good to great director. His mileage varies at times, and there are some movies that had the potential to be all time stone cold masterpieces, like Jarhead and Road to Perdition, that are still good films but didn't reach their full potential. It should also be noted that Mendes is also a stage director and spends much of his time there, so he's torn between two different art forms. He's talented in both, it's just a different flavor than someone like Nolan who does only movies (not to mention that it means he's made fewer movies than his contemporaries). 

All in all I can see him being someone's favorite director or in the top 10. In terms of all timer status, I'd say he has potential to be in the top 100, although how highly he goes will depend on how you measure greatness: vision, totality of his career, certain movies, etc.

Extremely capable and talented director. I wouldn't label him as legendary. He certainly hasn't ascended to the heights of Scorsese, Spielberg, Coppola, or Lee. He's not at Nolan's status, which is below the 4 I just listed. He actually reminds me of old Hollywood where there were directors who were solid and talented enough to make good films across different genres. You couldn't really discern a style or voice from their films.

Gotta be a troll post right? I don't think he's anywhere close to any of the 3 directors you mentioned. Of the films I've seen by him Skyfall is the clear standout the rest are poor to middling. None of them made any lasting impression, they're milquetoast and lack anything of important to say. Seemingly destined to play on TNT bloated with commercials before a NBA game.

He's easy above average in skill, but I feel like he doesn't have a lot to say. His movies seem important but I didn't feel like I gain any insight from his films or ever feel the need to watch them a second time. They're just fine, even though they are very well done. Like I do think 1917 was a pretty hollow exercise were his showboating hurt the potential for the film to be more emotional or two a better story. The gimmick took precedence. A truly great director wouldn't do something like that. He's like Ron Howard, but more pretentious.

I don’t think he’s quite reached legendary status but is a well-known director known for quality work. Not sure I’d say Christopher Nolan has really reached legendary status either tbh. Maybe in a decade or two. Just my opinion of course.
There are at least two notable directors named Lee. (Three, if you count Bruce's lone directorial effort.) Which one do you mean?
Haha, good point, although I love Bruce, but c'mon. Anyways, I was being American-centric so it's Lee, Spike Lee.

>However, I'm wondering if he truly stands among the greats like Spielberg, Scorsese, or Nolan, or if he's just a really good director who hasn't quite reached that legendary status. What do you all think? Is Sam Mendes one of the all-time great directors, or is he simply good but not great? Would love to hear your opinions and insights!

Well, what are the criteria for greatness? 

One possible data point we can use for a filmmaker's critical acclaim (which could be a proxy for greatness, or at least perceived greatness) is his or her performance on the 2022 BFI/*Sight and Sound Poll.* Mendes did not do well at all on this poll.

None of his films made the directors' top 100. In [this critics' poll, ](https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1gDnl2aIR17Sde-gJJ4NPRB7Vz0YYAEKCiLcreQvpuA8/edit?gid=1242179446#gid=1242179446)none of his films received more than a single vote. *1917* and *Road to Perdition* each received a single vote, finishing tied for 1,935th. This would seem to suggest that he is simply not thought of as an all-time great or canonical filmmaker by modern critics, and by a pretty overwhelming consensus.
I see. Ang Lee, of course, also being a very talented and capable filmmaker.

As someone who really likes some of Mendes' work, I don't think he's a legendary director. As others have said, his background in theater shows in his movies; consequentially, I think his strength as a stage director means he hasn't ever developed a distinct sense of cinematic style. 

I think Nolan hit legendary status after Inception and totally sealed it after Oppenheimer. He's at the spot Spielberg was at in the early 90s.

The thing about Nolan is that he does attract a more "serious" critical analysis than Spielberg was back then, which to me means he's likely to stay relevant longer. I know people on this sub like to make fun of Nolan fans for thinking that he's the second coming of Kubrick or whatever, but the fact that Nolan's $200 million dollar blockbusters even get talked about in that way is proof enough that he's much more than just a big commercial filmmaker.

I think Nolan is a good comparison for him tbh. They’re both masters of the mid-brow blockbuster. Their films don’t feel very personal, which to me is the main thing that keeps them at ‘good’ and stops them from being ‘great.’ 

But they can entertain you without making you feel like you just swallowed down slop, which isn’t nothing.
Is Ron Howard really thought of as a gimmicky director?
Not at all. I think he's very skilled but doesn't take himself as seriously as Mendes. He wouldn't do smelling like a one-shot gimmick if it limited the story. He isn't showing off.
Agree
Thanks I would consider him to be a great director but maybe not one of the greatest of all time
I'd put Ang over Spike any day
Road To Perdition is one of my all time favorites, way better than Jarhead

Neither. And Nolan is not one of the grear directors either. Nor Spielberg. 

I mean the great directors club would include:

- Murnau
- Eisenstein 
- Mizoguchi 
- Kurosawa 
- Hitchcock 
- Di Sica
- Ray

Names like that. Of the guys you mentioned only Scorsese is in that group.

No offense but if you go through film history more, you will realize this.

And if you were a little less self-important, you might appreciate that this is not a prize-giving for the best list. It is, after all, a matter of opinion, however well qualified an individual feels about making an offering about art.

Hmmm not self-important. I am recognizing the importance of the above mentioned guys.

So if its all opinion, shall we put Michael Bay in there?

Sure. A valid opinion. I appreciate his work very much and he is in the top tier of contemporary directors no question. I just don’t think he’s made it to legendary status. But as ‘legendary status’ is not strictly defined I guess we’ll have to agree to disagree. I think it’s a word like ‘genius’ that gets thrown around a little too liberally for my liking and I suppose that for me he’s simply too young and has made too few films to be accorded that honour. But I’m not dogmatic about it.
A lot of people wouldn’t describe Nolan as ‘among the greats’ either

He did perform significantly better than Mendes with critics, though: *The Dark Knight* in the top 500, *Inception* and *Interstellar* and *Memento* in the top 1,000, *The Prestige* and *Dunkirk* also getting votes.

His body of work is not expressive enough for him to be considered among the "all-time greats" in a broader sense (even though this criteria is ultimately subjective), but Mendes is an interesting filmmaker, with a background in theater. He won the Oscar for Best Director for his first film ("American Beauty"), and by that time he already had a long career on the West End and Broadway. That film is somewhat controversial nowadays and was picked as a possible "overrated" film that couldn't stand the test of time, but IMO it remains an extraordinary piece of cinema. I'm not so found of 1917, even though from a technical standpoint it's truly impressive.

Mendes is nowhere near as good or relevant as any of your first two examples, and he's certainly far less ambitious than Nolan. 

Mendes strikes me as the kind of director every big studio wants. Quite talented at his craft, can do middlebrow crowd pleasers that attract Oscar buzz, and delivers on time. He's a professional, a technician even, but a great artist? I  wouldn't go there. 

Even he admitted that his (once) most celebrated film, *American Beauty,* was not quite as good as people were making it out to be. It simply resonated with the times, and as the times changed it was just dismissed and somewhat forgotten just as swiftly.
I bet Spike could direct a solid Incredible Hulk film

I find his new film series, the 4 Beatles installments very interesting. I think the story device of 4 movies simultaneously happening, has potential to move the cinematic needle. I could see it going as far as a  Roshoman type of story where each character has a different take on the same events. And if the first 2 releases are knockouts at the blockbuster, audiences will be hooked to see how the series concludes.
True. 1917 is a good looking film, but you're right, the gimmick is just that, a gimmick, whereas in Dunkirk, the narrative device is integral to the film's strength and perspective.
If you manage to make a convincing case for him, why not? Just listing famous old directors in itself is not very compelling.
Lol old directors. Funny guy.

1917 is the sort of film that makes us think the cinematographer was calling the shots, and a popular gimmick after Inarritu's collaborations with Lubezki resulting in an Oscar galore. I will never forget the utter joy of seeing Mendes lose that Oscar to Bong Joon-Ho. American Beauty is a different game, though. That's an impressive achievement.

Is Spike Lee really in the same conversation as Scorsese and Spielberg? Lee’s done some great stuff but not at the same frequency as the others. 

Do the right thing is amazing but I’d put Tarantino ahead of him.
Hanks said that is one of the most important movies he made to him and nobody ever talks about it. It was a circus moment for his career, his words.

Mendes earned a ton of points with me for Skyfall since it’s my favourite Bond movie. He expanded on that with 1917 which was also great but he needs a few more absolute bangers for him to be put into more esteemed lists and frankly I don’t know if he has it in him.
Sam Mendes is a way better director than Nolan. That's crazy to me.

Howard is Hollywood-bred. He is skilled when it comes to classic narrative. IMO, it's not about how much one takes itself seriously, but their ability to take risks and experiment. I mean, Ron Howard adapted the most controversial book in the early 2000s (The DaVinci Code) into a movie so bland and unremarkable that we barely remember it at all.
As a fan of Nolan, I agree. I don't understand his inclusion with Spielberg and Scorsese.
I think they’re the same tier but Spike is flashier so people remember him more. That and DTRT is just iconic.

Yeah I'd agree re do the right thing. I'm not American, however, and I feel Spike Lee is strongly cultural in a way that Ang Lee isn't. Black Kkklansman and crouching tiger hidden dragon are neck and neck for me as well.
Kiyoshi Kurosawa mentioned 😱
Spielberg is one of the greats if you know anything about the filmmaking process. However, I'd agree that Nolan and especially Sam Mendes is nowhere near that status of "greatness".

Spielberg is not among the greats if you know anything about the final product.

Jaws and Schindler’s List. Maybe Jurassic Park. But that’s not enough. 3 films out of like 30+? No.
what do you mean by "final product"

It doesn’t matter what anyone else says or ranks, it’s what the movie means to you. The movies may not rank that high according to polls in other comments but just think how high they rank on your list. I fucking love the ones you mentioned. I also know that if a movie has a bigger directors name on it doesn’t mean it’s a 10. American Beauty was huge when it was released, it’s still a great movie. 1917 was a brilliant movie, separates it self from all the other world war flicks. Mendes is definitely greatness.
That's great to hear. It was also Newman's last role. I loved Hanks Newman and Jude Law in this. Mendes' directing was excellent too.
Finished film

Well there's many things that go into the finished product other than just what the director does. I don't know what your gripes with the majority of his films are (there are plenty to be had especially from the past 20 years) but, ignoring that I think there's many more great films in his catalogue than the ones you've mentioned, that doesn't mean he isn't one of most excellent DIRECTORS in not just the new hollywood but all of modern cinema. Maybe you have issues with the writing idk but that's separate. Just look up any number of videos on Spielberg's blocking and staging skills, his effortless one takes, and the camera techniques he uses to efficiently and stylishly \*direct\* the audience's attention. I mean, isn't that what a great director should do - direct the audience's attention in efficient, focused, purposeful, and thematically/characteristically relevant ways?

We judge films as a finished product. Anything else is ridiculous.

I don’t have gripes with him. Just he is not on the level of the likes of Murnau, Eisenstein, Gance, whoever…

Sorry I didn’t mean to upset you or anything. Just take it as my opinion and dismiss it…
I have a love-hate thing with Spike Lee; his contribution to cinema is immense and yet he’s so damn inconsistent.
A “one-take” ww1 film is not ambitious?
oh lol I'm not upset or anything I just find it interesting how Spielberg gets dismissed a lot nowadays

It’s difficult to say as I don’t know how much of film history you know.

But there are lots of people that don’t even get mentioned these days that I would put above him. I mean how many people talk about Pudovkin?

Yes, Spike belongs in the same category as those two. I think his subject matter tends to rub a certain sect of America the wrong way. I don’t think there has been a successful U.S. director as unique as him in the past 35 years.

As far as Tarantino, I don’t think it’s close. QT broke out of his somewhat one note film making with Once…Hollywood, but overall, he doesn’t match up.
[removed]

It is ambitious, of course, by the very nature of its conceit. But of all the one-take films I can recall; be it true one-shots like Russian Ark, Victoria or that really long sequence in *One Cut of the Dead*; or films cleverly edited to seem like it, such as Birdman; I can confidently say that 1917 is the one that plays it "safest." 

While very aesthetically pleasing (I mean, this is Roger Deakins we're talking about) and technically spotless (as expected from Mendes) there's very little in the way of thematic density, particularly complex imagery or narrative risk. 

It's a very literal film in which everything you see is exactly as presented and that, I'd argue, sanitizes its subject matter through its own overt artifice.
